text:
On their last trip to the beach, they brought a melon neither of them knew how to choose.

“It should sound hollow,” Simon said, knocking on it.

“So should a wall.”

Ruth lifted another and smelled the indentation where its stem had been. She had seen a woman do this in Italy, with an authority that made it seem less like shopping than diagnosis.

“What are you getting?”

“Nothing.”

“Then that one.”

They bought it, with bread, cheese, and almonds Simon opened before they reached the car.

For eleven days, they had been sleeping together in a room intended for the temporary production of art. It contained a narrow bed, a scarred desk, and framed evacuation procedures. Reaching for his glasses, Simon had knocked the frame down. Neither had replaced it.

They had not discussed Friday.

It was Wednesday.

Ruth drove. Simon offered, but she preferred having something to do with her hands. She was translating a novelist whose surviving son disputed every adjective suggesting his mother had been unhappy. Simon made films about places where something had ceased to exist. His current project concerned abandoned swimming pools.

“Do you ever swim in them?” someone had asked at dinner.

“Not generally.”

Ruth had liked him for not improving the answer.

Now he navigated from the director’s map.

“We passed it.”

“You said the next left.”

“That was the next left.”

“That was a driveway.”

“It had a sign.”

“The sign said Larsen.”

The driveway led to public parking behind a private house. Simon refrained from mentioning this.

A woman in a fluorescent vest approached.

“Sticker?”

“We’re at Bellwether,” Simon said.

She waited.

“The arts place.”

“Everybody’s somewhere.”

Without a sticker, they would have to use the town lot.

Back on the road, Simon said, “She seemed open to hearing more about the residency.”

Ruth laughed, and the morning loosened.

At Bellwether, they had been given five weeks to work without explaining why it mattered. At breakfast people asked what she was doing; at lunch, how it was going.

Ruth had a husband in London, although they no longer lived together. She had mentioned this early, to the table, while someone passed the plums. Simon had a daughter in Chicago. His phone lit up most afternoons with videos of a guinea pig performing no discernible action.

The first time he kissed Ruth, they had been looking for a moth. They found it behind a library curtain. Simon opened the window.

“You have to turn the lamp off,” she said.

In the dark, he touched her wrist. Later, she could not remember whether the moth escaped.

The path from the town lot crossed hot, yielding sand. Simon wore sandals he twice called a mistake. They passed a family heading back, the father carrying a collapsed tent as if it had been shot.

“Jellyfish,” a child informed them.

“All right,” Simon said.

“Millions.”

Twenty people occupied the beach at distances suggesting mutual disappointment. Ruth dropped the towels.

“Too close,” Simon said.

“To what?”

“The water.”

The tide appeared to be a quarter of a mile away.

“Is it coming in?”

“I assume it does that.”

They moved uphill.

For a while they were quiet. Ruth had liked this about him. Increasingly, though, she distinguished between shared silence and two people waiting for the other to speak.

Simon took out his phone.

“Work?”

“Mae.”

His daughter held the guinea pig against her chest.

“His name’s Dennis.”

“I know.”

“Right.”

Ruth knew the cage was in Mae’s bedroom, that Simon’s former wife objected to the smell, and that Simon had suggested different bedding.

He watched the video again.

Ruth removed her shirt.

“Well. We came here.”

The jellyfish lay scattered along the shore, smaller than the child had suggested but considerably more numerous. Simon stopped to photograph one.

“Will this go in the film?”

“No.”

“Just a personal jellyfish.”

He lowered his phone. “Is that annoying?”

“No.”

The water was cold enough to make Ruth feel misinformed. She plunged forward and surfaced with hair across her mouth. Simon remained knee-deep.

“Come on.”

“I’m happy here.”

“You look ecstatic.”

He waved.

She swam past a dark raft of seaweed. There was pleasure in being briefly unavailable to him. From the water his body was ordinary and dear: narrow shoulders, the soft middle he apologised for through jokes. She wanted him to join her. She also wanted him to stay and watch.

When she returned, he held out her towel. She stepped into it, and he wrapped her shoulders. For a moment she pressed her forehead to his chest. His shirt smelled of the residency’s detergent, a smell he would not have anywhere else.

“We should eat,” he said.

The melon resisted the borrowed kitchen knife. Simon sawed while Ruth held it steady. At last the rind split.

Inside, the fruit was almost white.

“Maybe that’s the variety.”

They tried a piece. It tasted of cucumber and refrigerator.

“Excellent choice,” Ruth said.

“Beautifully fragrant.”

They ate bread and cheese. A gull approached sideways, pretending to have business elsewhere.

“What time’s your train Friday?” Ruth asked.

“Ten-forty.”

“Mine’s eleven.”

“We could share a car.”

“Yes. That makes sense.”

“And you’re going straight home?”

“For a few days. Then my sister’s.”

“Right.”

“My sister thinks I should get a flat.”

“Do you want to?”

“I want to not have to buy a kettle.”

He smiled, but she meant it. Choosing the objects for another life exhausted her. She could imagine leaving her husband more readily than owning a second draining board.

“Mae starts school Monday,” Simon said.

“You’ll be back.”

“That’s the plan.”

There was nothing wrong with this exchange. That was part of what made her want to cry.

A gust sent the almond packet skittering away. Simon chased it. Each time he bent down, it moved again. Ruth watched with an irritation that became tenderness.

When he returned, breathless, she said, “Heroic.”

“It was getting personal.”

He sat too close to the melon and put his hand into it.

She laughed until he began laughing too, still examining his wet palm.

By two, clouds covered the beach. They packed badly. Simon wanted to save the melon.

“For whom?”

“Someone might—”

“Simon.”

He carried it to a bin.

Ruth forgot her shoes and went back. Their place was occupied by a woman helping an elderly man into a sweater. One shoe lay sideways; the other had filled with sand.

At the car, Simon held the keys.

“It won’t start.”

“You tried?”

“I thought I’d just establish a mood.”

She turned the key. Dry clicks.

The headlights had been on.

Neither assigned blame. Ruth remembered switching them on beneath the trees. Simon remembered nothing, an advantage he was kind enough not to use.

The director did not answer. Roadside assistance could not locate their membership. Simon went for help.

Ruth sat with both doors open. On Friday she would pack her swimsuit damp and open it somewhere else.

Her husband had messaged that morning: did she want the desk?

They had bought it from a man whose wife was moving into care. She remembered waiting while he searched for the drawer key. Her husband had said they didn’t need it. The man kept searching.

She typed, *Yes, if you don’t mind.*

Then deleted the last four words.

Simon returned with a retired electrician named Paul, who had cables and an expansive theory about batteries. Paul’s wife waited in their truck.

“Nice day for it,” she told Ruth.

“It was.”

“You go in?”

“Yes.”

“Not me.”

The engine caught immediately.

Back on the road, neither wanted music.

“We could stop,” Simon said.

“For what?”

“Coffee.”

“There’s coffee at the house.”

“I know.”

They stopped beside a hardware store. Simon ordered two coffees and apple cake.

“I don’t want cake,” Ruth said.

“I do.”

He pushed the plate between them. She ate some.

Outside, a man struggled to fit a pipe into a hatchback.

“I’m not good at this part,” Simon said.

She waited.

“The end.”

“We’ve got two days.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t get ahead.”

He looked down. She had rebuked him for saying what she wanted him to say.

“I’m not good at it either,” she said.

They watched the man open his passenger door.

“Do you want to come to Chicago?”

“Yes.” Then, “I don’t know when.”

“All right.”

“You could come to London.”

“I could.”

Neither reached for a calendar. She was relieved, and ashamed of her relief.

Simon slept on the drive back. At a traffic light Ruth lowered his sun visor, although there was no sun.

At Bellwether, a notice requested that residents label anything they wanted before Friday’s refrigerator clean-out.

Ruth showered. Downstairs, Simon was washing the knife. He had put away the bread and cheese.

“The melon?” she asked.

“Gone.”

She dried the knife.

“I’ll get the towels,” he said.

“Leave them. I’m doing a wash.”

He fetched his clothes, bundled in a shirt. Checking his pockets, she found a receipt, a tissue, and a white stone.

She carried the stone to him.

“Yours?”

“I forgot about that.”

“Do you want it?”

“Yes.”

He held out his hand, and she put it there.
